title: HCF and LCM Fundamentals
tagline: Year 1 Foundation — Greatest Common Factor & Least Common Multiple

introduction.overview: HCF (Highest Common Factor) and LCM (Least Common Multiple) are two of the most important operations in elementary number theory. They model real-world problems of equal division, scheduling, tiling, and concurrent events. HCF and LCM questions are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds.
introduction.placementRelevance: HCF and LCM are commonly tested directly in company aptitude rounds and are embedded in work/time, distance/time, and fraction problems. The fundamental identity HCF×LCM = A×B is the fastest tool for finding missing values.
introduction.realWorldContext: Operating systems use LCM for scheduling CPU tasks at equal intervals. Network protocols use HCF to align data packet sizes. Civil engineers use HCF to cut materials into maximum equal-sized pieces. LCM governs synchronization of repeating processes.

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Be able to write a number as a product of primes and to test divisibility quickly.

coreDefinitions: HCF (Highest Common Factor): The largest integer that divides two or more given numbers exactly. Also called GCD (Greatest Common Divisor). HCF(12, 18) = 6.
LCM (Least Common Multiple): The smallest positive integer that is divisible by two or more given numbers. LCM(4, 6) = 12.
Key Identity: HCF(A,B) × LCM(A,B) = A × B — fundamental for solving problems when 3 of the 4 values are known.
Co-prime numbers: HCF = 1, so LCM = A × B.
HCF ≤ min(A,B) and LCM ≥ max(A,B) — use these inequalities to eliminate impossible options.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: HCF answers: 'What is the largest equal unit I can cut both A and B into?' LCM answers: 'What is the smallest time when both periodic events A and B coincide?' These framings make problem identification instant: equal distribution/cutting → HCF; scheduling/cycling → LCM.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: HCF = intersection of prime factor sets (minimum exponents of COMMON primes). LCM = union of prime factor sets (maximum exponents of ALL primes). Visualize: HCF(36,48): 36=2²×3², 48=2⁴×3 → common primes are 2 and 3 → take min powers: HCF=2²×3=12. LCM: take max powers: 2⁴×3²=144.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: HCF × LCM = A × B
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Fundamental identity — works for exactly TWO numbers only.
importantRulesAndFormulas.whenToUse: When 3 of the 4 quantities are known.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: HCF by Prime Factorization
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: HCF = product of LOWEST powers of COMMON prime factors
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Factorize both numbers, take minimum exponent of each shared prime.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: LCM by Prime Factorization
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: LCM = product of HIGHEST powers of ALL prime factors
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Collect all primes from both numbers with maximum exponent.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: HCF by Euclidean Algorithm
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: HCF(A,B) = HCF(B, A mod B), repeat until remainder=0
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Efficient for large numbers. Last non-zero remainder is HCF.
importantRulesAndFormulas.whenToUse: Large numbers where factorization is slow.

mainNarrative: HCF finds the maximum equal unit. If you want to cut a 48 m rope and a 36 m rope into the largest possible equal pieces with no leftover, each piece must be HCF(48, 36) = 12 m, giving 4 pieces from the first and 3 from the second — 7 total, zero waste. The HCF is the 'common measure' that divides both quantities perfectly.

LCM finds the minimum common cycle. If Bus A departs every 12 minutes and Bus B every 18 minutes, and both depart at 9:00 AM, they next depart together after LCM(12, 18) = 36 minutes — at 9:36 AM. LCM is the 'first point of synchronization' of two or more repeating events.

The product formula HCF×LCM = A×B is the most powerful shortcut in this chapter. When any three of the four quantities are known, substitute and solve for the fourth in a single step. Many placement questions give HCF and LCM and ask for a second number given the first — do not factorize; use the formula directly.
For three or more numbers: HCF(A,B,C) = HCF(HCF(A,B), C) and LCM(A,B,C) = LCM(LCM(A,B), C). The product formula CANNOT be extended to three numbers — it strictly applies to pairs only.

deepDiveAspects.title: Euclidean Algorithm — Mathematical Basis
deepDiveAspects.content: The algorithm uses the fact that HCF(A,B) = HCF(B, A mod B). This holds because any common divisor of A and B must also divide A − B, A − 2B, …, and ultimately A mod B (which is A minus some multiple of B). Repeated application reduces the problem until one value becomes 0, at which point the other equals the HCF. For HCF(1071, 462): 1071=2×462+147 → HCF(462,147): 462=3×147+21 → HCF(147,21): 147=7×21+0 → HCF=21.

deepDiveAspects.title: HCF/LCM Problem Type Recognition Guide
deepDiveAspects.content: Type 1 — Equal distribution/Maximum equal piece: HCF. Example: 'Largest tiles to cover floor without cutting'. Type 2 — Scheduling/When do they meet again: LCM. Example: 'When do three bells ring together'. Type 3 — 'Largest number that divides A, B, C leaving same remainder R': HCF(A−R, B−R, C−R). Type 4 — 'Smallest number divisible by A and B': LCM. Type 5 — 'Smallest number that when divided by A and B leaves remainder R': LCM(A,B)+R.

problemVariations.description: Find maximum equal-size groups from two or more quantities.
problemVariations.exampleSnippet: Two pieces of ribbon 48m and 36m — find maximum equal piece length.

problemVariations.description: Find when two or more periodic events first coincide.
problemVariations.exampleSnippet: Bells ring every 4, 6, 9 minutes — when do they ring together?

problemVariations.description: Use HCF×LCM=A×B to find an unknown.
problemVariations.exampleSnippet: HCF=11, LCM=693, one number=77. Find the other.

solvedExamples.title: Finding Missing Number Using HCF×LCM = A×B
solvedExamples.question: The HCF of two numbers is 11 and their LCM is 693. If one number is 77, find the other.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The product formula is the fastest route when 3 of the 4 values (HCF, LCM, A, B) are known.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Manually finding LCM instead of using the formula — wastes 40+ seconds.

solvedExamples.title: Three Bells Ringing Together — LCM Application
solvedExamples.question: Three bells ring at intervals of 12, 15, and 20 minutes. If they all ring together at 6:00 AM, when do they next ring together?
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Next simultaneous ring = after LCM(12, 15, 20) minutes.

steps.title: LCM = max power of each prime

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: LCM gives the minimum time that is a multiple of all three intervals — the first simultaneous occurrence.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Adding intervals (12+15+20=47) or multiplying them instead of computing LCM.

solvedExamples.title: Least number leaving the same remainder
solvedExamples.question: Find the least number which, when divided by 6, 9 and 15, leaves a remainder of 4 in each case.
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Required number = LCM of the divisors + common remainder.

steps.title: Add the remainder
steps.explanation: The number is a multiple of 90 plus 4. The least such number is 90 + 4 = 94.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: A multiple of the LCM leaves remainder 0 for every divisor, so adding 4 leaves remainder 4 for each.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Giving the LCM (90) as the answer.

shortcutMethods.title: HCF and LCM Speed Methods

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: List all factors of each number and pick the greatest common one (slow for large numbers).
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Euclidean algorithm for HCF (4–6 steps). Product formula HCF×LCM=A×B to find missing values instantly.

rulesForApplication: Co-prime numbers: HCF=1, so LCM = A×B directly.
Product formula works ONLY for TWO numbers — do not use for three.
Smallest number divisible by A and B leaving remainder R: LCM(A,B) + R.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: HCF×LCM = A×B strictly holds for TWO numbers only.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: For 3 numbers, find HCF or LCM step by step: HCF(HCF(A,B),C).

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing HCF and LCM problem types
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Applying LCM where HCF is needed.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Equal cutting/maximum divisor → HCF. Scheduling/minimum common cycle → LCM.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Dividing smaller by larger in the first step.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Always divide LARGER by SMALLER. HCF(A,B) where A>B: compute A mod B, then HCF(B, A mod B).

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: HCF MCQs: answer must divide both given numbers. LCM MCQs: answer must be divisible by both. These filters instantly eliminate 2–3 options.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Identify problem type first (equal cutting → HCF; scheduling → LCM). Then choose Euclidean algorithm or product formula depending on what information is given.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: HCF/LCM is tested in TCS NQT, Infosys Intellect, and Cognizant GenC aptitude rounds. It also appears embedded in work/time and pipes problems.

summaryBullets: HCF = largest common divisor (equal cutting). LCM = smallest common multiple (scheduling).
HCF×LCM = A×B — works for TWO numbers only.
HCF: min powers of common primes. LCM: max powers of all primes.
Euclidean: HCF(A,B)=HCF(B, A mod B) — fastest for large numbers.
Smallest N leaving remainder R when divided by A and B: LCM(A,B)+R.
quickFormulas: Smallest N divisible by A,B leaving R: LCM(A,B)+R

keyTakeaways: The product formula HCF×LCM=A×B is the single most useful shortcut in this chapter.
Always identify problem type first: equal cutting → HCF; cycling/scheduling → LCM.
The Euclidean algorithm handles any size numbers in 4–6 steps — practise until it is reflexive.
selfCheckQuestions: Find HCF(252,105) using Euclidean algorithm. Show every step.
Two lights blink every 8 and 12 seconds. When do they next blink together?
HCF of 24 and 36 is 12. Find LCM using the formula only.
